table.caption: Velor, an invented country with a natural rate of unemployment of 5 percent

phillips-curve-s2.title: A spending boom in Lumen (invented country)
phillips-curve-s2.text: Lumen, an invented country, is in long-run equilibrium. Its unemployment rate equals the natural rate of 4 percent, and actual and expected inflation are both 2 percent. Then a boom in stock prices makes households feel richer, and consumption rises sharply. Lumen's government and central bank take no action.

items.q: Label the axes and both curves of the Phillips curve graph.

why.correct: The inflation rate is on the vertical axis and the unemployment rate on the horizontal axis; SRPC slopes down and LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

items.q: The economy starts where SRPC crosses LRPC. Then consumer spending rises, shifting AD right. Place point B to show where the economy moves in the short run.

why.correct: An AD shift is a movement along the SRPC: higher output means lower unemployment, and the faster rise in prices means higher inflation, so B is up and to the left on the same SRPC.

items.q: A sharp rise in world oil prices raises production costs for firms across the economy. Shift the right curve to show the effect on the Phillips curves.

why.correct: A negative supply shock shifts SRAS left on the AD-AS graph, which raises both inflation and unemployment: the SRPC shifts right. The natural rate is unchanged, so LRPC stays put.

key.because: a negative supply shock (higher oil prices)

slips.LRPC: A supply shock does not change the natural rate of unemployment, so LRPC stays where it is. The short-run trade-off gets worse, so SRPC shifts.

items.q: After years of rising prices, workers and firms come to expect a higher inflation rate. Shift the right curve and mark the new long-run equilibrium where the curves cross.

why.correct: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC right (up). Where SRPC2 meets LRPC, unemployment is at the natural rate and inflation equals the new, higher expected rate.

slips.LRPC: Expected inflation changes the short-run trade-off; the natural rate of unemployment, and so LRPC, does not depend on it.

items.q: Between which two years did Velor most likely move along a single short-run Phillips curve after a rise in AD?
options: Year 1 to Year 2
Year 2 to Year 3
Year 3 to Year 4
Year 1 to Year 3

why.correct: Along a given SRPC, unemployment and inflation move in opposite directions. Only Year 1 to Year 2 fits.
options: Right: unemployment fell and inflation rose, the inverse short-run trade-off a rise in AD produces.
Both unemployment and inflation rose; a movement along one SRPC changes them in opposite directions.
Both rose again, which points to a shift of the SRPC, not a movement along it.
Unemployment is the same in both years while inflation is higher, so the economy is on a different SRPC.

items.q: In Year 3, unemployment is back at the natural rate, but inflation is 4 percent instead of the 2 percent of Year 1. What best explains this?
options: The natural rate of unemployment fell, so LRPC shifted left and inflation rose along it
AD fell, so the economy moved down along the SRPC toward higher inflation
Expected inflation rose, so the SRPC shifted right and the economy returned to LRPC at a higher inflation rate
A positive supply shock shifted the SRPC left, raising inflation

why.correct: In the long run the economy is on LRPC at the natural rate, and inflation equals expected inflation. A higher inflation rate at the natural rate means expected inflation rose.
options: Unemployment is still 5 percent, the stated natural rate, so LRPC did not move.
A fall in AD moves the economy down the SRPC to lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Right: once people expect higher inflation, the SRPC crosses LRPC at that higher rate, so unemployment returns to 5 percent with inflation at 4 percent.
A leftward SRPC shift lowers inflation at each unemployment rate.

items.q: From Year 3 to Year 4, both unemployment and inflation rose. Which event fits that change?
options: A rise in government spending on roads that shifted AD right
A sharp rise in energy prices that shifted SRAS left
A fall in consumer confidence that shifted AD left
A fall in the natural rate of unemployment

why.correct: When inflation and unemployment rise together, the SRPC has shifted right; a negative supply shock is the usual cause.
options: More AD lowers unemployment while it raises inflation.
Right: a negative supply shock raises the price level and lowers output, so inflation and unemployment rise together.
Less AD lowers inflation while it raises unemployment.
A lower natural rate would let unemployment fall, not rise, in the long run.

items.q: Using the table, what is Velor's cyclical unemployment rate in Year 4?

why.correct: Actual = natural + cyclical, so cyclical $= 6.5 - 5.0 = 1.5$ percent. Positive cyclical unemployment means the economy is to the right of LRPC.

mistakes.why: That is the actual unemployment rate. Cyclical unemployment is the part above the natural rate: 6.5 - 5.0.
You added the natural rate. The actual rate is natural plus cyclical, so subtract: 6.5 - 5.0.

items.q: What happens to Lumen's unemployment and inflation rates in the short run?
options: Unemployment rises above 4 percent, and inflation rises above 2 percent
Unemployment falls below 4 percent, and inflation falls below 2 percent
Unemployment stays at 4 percent, and inflation rises above 2 percent
Unemployment falls below 4 percent, and inflation rises above 2 percent

why.correct: A rise in AD moves the economy up and to the left along the SRPC.
options: Both rising together is a supply shock, a shift of the SRPC. Here AD rose.
More spending raises prices faster, not slower.
That describes the long run. In the short run, higher AD raises output and lowers unemployment.
Right: higher consumption shifts AD right, so output rises (unemployment falls) and prices rise faster (inflation rises): a movement up along the SRPC.

items.q: Households and firms in Lumen come to expect the higher inflation rate. Where does the economy end up in the long run?
options: Below 4 percent unemployment, with inflation back at 2 percent
At 4 percent unemployment, with inflation above 2 percent, on a new SRPC
At 4 percent unemployment, with inflation back down at the old 2 percent
Above 4 percent unemployment, with inflation below 2 percent

why.correct: In the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate whatever the inflation rate, which is why LRPC is vertical. Higher expected inflation leaves the economy on LRPC at a higher inflation rate.
options: Unemployment cannot stay below the natural rate in the long run; LRPC is vertical at 4 percent.
Right: as expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts right, and the economy returns to LRPC at the natural rate with the higher inflation.
Inflation returns to 2 percent only if expectations stay at 2 percent. Here people now expect higher inflation.
That is where a fall in AD would push the economy in the short run.

items.q: Which change on Lumen's AD-AS graph matches its long-run adjustment?
options: Nominal wages rise with expected inflation, so SRAS shifts left until output is back at full employment
Nominal wages fall, so SRAS shifts right and output rises further above full employment
LRAS shifts right to meet the higher level of output
AD keeps shifting right until the price level stops rising

why.correct: The two graphs tell one story: the SRAS shift left on the AD-AS graph is the SRPC shift right on the Phillips curve graph.
options: Right: higher expected inflation raises nominal wages and input prices; SRAS shifts left, output returns to full employment and the SRPC shifts right.
With unemployment below the natural rate, wages rise, not fall.
Full-employment output depends on resources and technology; a spending boom does not move it.
More AD would push output further from full employment; the long-run adjustment comes from SRAS.

items.q: Build the chain for Lumen, from the spending boom to the long run.

why.correct: AD rises, the economy moves along the SRPC to lower unemployment and higher inflation, then rising expected inflation shifts the SRPC right and unemployment returns to the natural rate.

specific.frame: Consumption rises, so AD shifts ___. Unemployment ___ and inflation rises: a movement ___ the SRPC. As expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts ___, and unemployment returns to ___.
specific.model: Consumption rises, so AD shifts right. Unemployment falls and inflation rises, which is a movement along the SRPC. Because expected inflation then rises, the SRPC shifts right, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 4 percent.

direction.label: Which way AD shifts
options: right
left

why.1: More consumption is more spending at each price level: a shift right.

unemployment.label: Unemployment in the short run
options: falls
rises

why.1: Higher output needs more workers, so unemployment falls.

link.label: Movement or shift
options: along
of

why.1: An AD change moves the economy along the SRPC; it does not shift it.

curve.label: Which way the SRPC shifts
options: right
left

why.1: Higher expected inflation raises inflation at each unemployment rate: a shift right (up).

trend.label: The long-run unemployment rate
options: the natural rate of 4 percent
a rate below 4 percent

why.1: LRPC is vertical at the natural rate; unemployment cannot stay below it in the long run.

items.q: Better job-search websites help unemployed workers find matching jobs faster, so the natural rate of unemployment falls. Shift the right curve.

why.correct: A lower natural rate moves the vertical LRPC to the left (and LRAS to the right on the AD-AS graph).

key.because: a fall in the natural rate of unemployment

items.q: The economy starts where SRPC crosses LRPC. Then business investment falls sharply, shifting AD left. Place point B to show the short-run result.

why.correct: A fall in AD is a movement down and to the right along the SRPC: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

items.q: What does the vertical long-run Phillips curve show?
options: In the long run, higher inflation keeps unemployment permanently lower
In the long run, the inflation rate is fixed whatever the unemployment rate
In the long run, unemployment is at the natural rate at any inflation rate
In the long run, unemployment falls to zero when inflation is high enough

why.correct: LRPC is the Phillips curve version of LRAS: both are vertical at full employment, where unemployment equals the natural rate.
options: That is the short-run trade-off. It disappears once expected inflation catches up.
A fixed inflation rate would be a horizontal line. LRPC fixes unemployment, not inflation.
Right: once expectations adjust there is no lasting trade-off, so LRPC is vertical at the natural rate.
Frictional and structural unemployment remain at any inflation rate; that is the natural rate.

items.q: Select every event that shifts the short-run Phillips curve to the right.
options: A rise in expected inflation
A rise in the price of oil used across the economy
A rise in government spending
A fall in consumer spending

why.correct: Supply shocks and changes in expected inflation shift the SRPC; changes in AD move the economy along it.
options: Right: higher expected inflation raises inflation at each unemployment rate.
Right: a negative supply shock shifts SRAS left and the SRPC right.
That shifts AD right: a movement along the SRPC, not a shift.
That shifts AD left: a movement down the SRPC.

items.q: A new technology sharply lowers energy costs for firms (a positive supply shock). What happens on the Phillips curve graph in the short run?
options: The SRPC shifts right: inflation and unemployment both rise
The economy moves up along the SRPC: inflation rises and unemployment falls
LRPC shifts right: the natural rate of unemployment rises
The SRPC shifts left: inflation and unemployment both fall

why.correct: A positive supply shock is the mirror image of a negative one: SRAS right, SRPC left.
options: That is a negative supply shock, such as a rise in oil prices.
A movement along the SRPC comes from a change in AD.
Cheaper energy does not raise the natural rate; the short-run curve moves.
Right: SRAS shifts right, so the price level rises more slowly and output rises; inflation and unemployment fall together.

items.q: Which feature of the AD-AS model matches the long-run Phillips curve?
options: SRAS, which slopes up
LRAS, vertical at full-employment output
AD, which slopes down
The point where AD crosses SRAS in the short run

why.correct: LRAS and LRPC both mark full employment: real GDP at potential, unemployment at the natural rate.
options: SRAS shifts match SRPC shifts in the opposite direction; it is not the long-run curve.
Right: full-employment output on LRAS is the output at which unemployment equals the natural rate, where LRPC stands.
AD shifts are movements along the SRPC.
That is the short-run equilibrium, which can sit off LRPC.
